vo.text: In 1187, a sultan lured an entire army out into the hills in the middle of summer. And then he waited for it to get thirsty.
The sultan was Saladin, ruler of Egypt and Syria. For almost ninety years, crusaders from Europe had held Jerusalem, and a string of castles along the coast.
That summer, Saladin attacked the town of Tiberias, by the Sea of Galilee. It was bait. He wanted the crusader army to come out and rescue it.
Some crusader lords said: don't go. It's July. There's no water on the way. Even the lord whose own wife was trapped in Tiberias said: don't go. King Guy of Jerusalem marched anyway.
About twenty thousand crusaders set out across the dry hills. In heavy armour. In July.
All day long, Saladin's horse archers rode around them, shooting arrows and blocking the way to water.
By evening, the crusaders were stuck on a dry plateau. Saladin's army stood between them and the lake. They could see the water. They just couldn't reach it.
That night, Saladin's men set fire to the dry grass. The smoke blew straight into the crusader camp. Thirsty, and now coughing.
In the morning, the crusaders tried to break through toward the springs, near two hills called the Horns of Hattin.
Their army broke into pieces. Some charged. Some fled up the hills. King Guy's red tent was surrounded on the Horns.
When the red tent fell, the battle was over. King Guy was captured.
Saladin offered the exhausted king a cup of water, cooled with ice. A sign that his life would be spared.
Three months later, Saladin took Jerusalem. And unlike the crusaders who had taken the city in 1099, he took it without a massacre.
Europe sent a new crusade, led by Richard the Lionheart. But Jerusalem stayed in Saladin's hands.
The lesson of Hattin: never cross dry hills in July. Especially in a metal suit.
